documents.title: What is a SIP (Systematic Investment Plan)
documents.text: A SIP (Systematic Investment Plan) lets you invest a fixed amount in a mutual fund at regular intervals such as monthly, weekly, or quarterly. It helps you build an investment gradually without needing a large lump sum upfront, and it averages your purchase price across market levels.

documents.title: What is an expense ratio
documents.text: The expense ratio is the annual fee a mutual fund charges to manage your investment, expressed as a percentage of the amount you have invested. A lower expense ratio means more of your money stays invested. It is deducted from the scheme's NAV, so you never pay it separately.

documents.title: What is an exit load
documents.text: An exit load is a fee charged when you redeem mutual fund units before a specified holding period. It is designed to discourage very early withdrawals. Once the exit load period ends, redemption is free of that charge.

documents.title: What is NAV (Net Asset Value)
documents.text: NAV (Net Asset Value) is the per-unit price of a mutual fund scheme. It is calculated at the end of every business day from the scheme's total assets minus liabilities, divided by the number of units outstanding. When you invest, units are allotted to you at the applicable NAV.

documents.title: What is ELSS (Equity Linked Savings Scheme)
documents.text: ELSS (Equity Linked Savings Scheme) is a category of mutual fund that invests primarily in equities and qualifies for a tax deduction under Section 80C of the Income Tax Act, up to Rs. 1.5 lakh per financial year. Every ELSS investment carries a mandatory 3-year lock-in.

documents.title: Difference between Direct and Regular plans
documents.text: A Direct plan is bought straight from the AMC and carries no distributor commission, so its expense ratio is lower. A Regular plan is bought through a distributor or advisor whose commission is built into the expense ratio. Both plans hold exactly the same portfolio; only the cost and therefore the NAV differ.

documents.title: What is the SEBI riskometer
documents.text: The riskometer is a SEBI-mandated risk label displayed on every mutual fund scheme. It has six levels: Low, Low to Moderate, Moderate, Moderately High, High, and Very High. AMCs review and disclose the riskometer level for each scheme every month.

documents.title: What is an SWP (Systematic Withdrawal Plan)
documents.text: An SWP (Systematic Withdrawal Plan) lets you withdraw a fixed amount from your mutual fund holding at regular intervals, the mirror image of a SIP. Units are redeemed at the applicable NAV on each withdrawal date, and exit load or lock-in rules still apply.

documents.title: What is an STP (Systematic Transfer Plan)
documents.text: An STP (Systematic Transfer Plan) moves a fixed amount from one mutual fund scheme to another at regular intervals, usually from a debt or liquid scheme into an equity scheme. Each transfer counts as a redemption from the source scheme, so exit load and tax rules apply to it.

documents.title: KYC requirement for mutual fund investing
documents.text: KYC (Know Your Customer) verification is mandatory before you can invest in any mutual fund in India. It is completed once through a KRA (KYC Registration Agency) and is then valid across all AMCs. You can check or complete your KYC status through CAMS, KFintech, or any SEBI-registered KRA.

documents.title: How equity mutual funds are taxed
documents.text: Gains on equity mutual funds held for more than 12 months are treated as long-term capital gains, and gains on units held for 12 months or less are short-term capital gains. The applicable rates and exemption limits are set by the Income Tax Act and change from time to time, so confirm the current rates with the Income Tax Department or a tax professional before filing.
